question: can a fixed step work at all for the high-k end of the workload?
method: numpy, one trajectory at k = 5 h/Mpc (mapped to 1/Mpc through the first cosmology's h), compared against the production adaptive driver
verdict: A FIXED STEP CANNOT WORK AT HIGH k.
the_most_important_detail: At dlna = 1.65e-4 the run never produced a NaN - it completed 97686 steps and returned dc = 2.2e79 against the adaptive 2.1e5, i.e. wrong by 74 orders of magnitude. So 'the array is finite' is NOT evidence of convergence, and the earlier NaN-based detection was too weak: it would have passed this run. Any future check must compare against a reference, not test for NaN.
where_it_breaks: Both divergences happen at a ~ 1.2e-4, deep in the radiation era and long before recombination. That is the regime the adaptive driver handles by shrinking its step dramatically; a uniform grid steps straight through it.
why_refining_does_not_rescue_it: the CFL limiter in the numpy driver is a per-step, per-trajectory quantity (angular CFL, dlna_nu, event distance). Over one trajectory it spans orders of magnitude, and over a batch it would have to be global. Taking the global minimum over the whole integration is what makes the uniform step unaffordable; taking anything coarser diverges.

established: rhs_torch is bit-identical to the numpy rhs (0 of 229 rows)
the GPU rhs is 3.76x faster at T=16384 and 10x slower at T=128
per-step cost is essentially FLAT from T=128 (73 ms) to T=16384 (61 ms), so batching is nearly free
what_this_does_to_the_gpu_plan.blocked: a batched device integrator needs ONE step for all trajectories, and no single step covers k from 0.05 (needs 1.84e-3) to 5 (needs well under 1.65e-4, and the pre-recombination phase needs less still)
what_this_does_to_the_gpu_plan.the_architectural_conflict_in_one_line: GPU batching wants a single global step; the physics wants per-trajectory adaptive control spanning orders of magnitude

options_this_leaves.note: each trajectory chooses its own step inside the kernel; correct, but SIMT divergence means the batch pays the slowest member anyway unless trajectories are re-packed, and that is a substantial kernel project

options_this_leaves.option: split the workload by k across backends
options_this_leaves.note: low k on the batched device path, high k on the CPU. Legitimate - no physics is dropped - but the cost is dominated by high k (97627 steps against 8752), so this saves little

options_this_leaves.option: keep the GPU work at the operator level only
options_this_leaves.note: use the verified 3.76x rhs as a building block called from the CPU adaptive driver. That reintroduces a host sync per step, which the measurements say is exactly what kills it

options_this_leaves.option: stop the GPU line and return to the accuracy target
options_this_leaves.note: the 0.5% nonlinear requirement is still unmet at 0.88% (HMcode) and 4.2-6.4% (end to end), and the GPU line has not changed that number at all

what_may_be_claimed: rhs_torch correctness (0/229) and the 3.76x operator-level speedup at T=16384
three latent batching bugs found and fixed (coefficient dict 2051.5 MiB -> 3.6 MiB)
a negative result: fixed-step device integration cannot cover this workload
what_may_not_be_claimed: any end-to-end GPU speedup - the only T=16384 run was NaN, and the fine-step run at k=5 was wrong by 74 orders of magnitude
that the GPU path is close to working - it is not; the integrator scheme itself is the blocker
